coldOpen: Some barcode bars are longer, and that's deliberate.
centralQuestion: Why are a few bars on a UPC barcode longer than the rest?

sources.name: GS1 US — UPCs, barcodes and prefixes

evidence.claim: The start, middle and end guard bars of a UPC-A barcode extend further down than the digit bars.
evidence.quote: The bars forming the S (start), M (middle), and E (end) guard patterns, are extended downwards

evidence.claim: Guard patterns do not encode a digit; they help decoding.
evidence.quote: not encoding a digit) are intermixed to help decoding

evidence.claim: The guard patterns separate the two groups of six digits and establish the timing.
evidence.quote: The guard patterns separate the two groups of six numerical digits and establish the timing

evidence.claim: A UPC-A barcode has exactly 30 bars: 6 form guard patterns and 24 represent its 12 digits.
evidence.quote: all UPC-A barcodes consist of exactly (3 × 2) + (12 × 2) = 30 bars, of which 6 represent guard patterns and 24 represent numerical digits

evidence.claim: IBM assigned George Laurer to determine how to make a supermarket scanner and label.
evidence.quote: assigned George Laurer to determine how to make a supermarket scanner and label

evidence.claim: Laurer and a colleague defined guard bars and how a scanner should detect the label.
evidence.quote: Together they defined guard bars and a definition of how to detect the label

evidence.claim: The guard bars also identified which half of the label was being read and trained the scanner's threshold circuits.
evidence.quote: The guard bars also provided identification for half label discrimination and training bars for the scanner threshold circuits

evidence.claim: Splitting the label into two halves allowed the bars to be cut nearly in half in length.
evidence.quote: suggested if the label were split into two halves the bar lengths could be cut nearly in half

evidence.claim: The first UPC-marked item scanned at a retail checkout was Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum in Troy, Ohio, on 26 June 1974.
evidence.quote: Wrigley's Juicy Fruit chewing gum, purchased at the Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio
